entries.text: Class name completion suggests only the `Core` classes and the classes in the folders that your program's `autoload` lines name. In a file that no program loads, it suggests every class.
When you rename a property, the name that `initProperty`, `onPropertyGet`, `onPropertySet` and `beforePropertySet` compare as a string changes too. Find references lists that string.
The warning `W1039` shows a string that a property method compares with the property name, when the class has no property with that name. Such a typo would only fail when the program runs.

A rename can move a class to another namespace. Write its full new name, such as `Shop\Billing\Cart`. Every `use` line changes, and the file moves to the folder that `autoload` reads for the new name.

When you move a class file to another folder with `nvs code move` or in the editor, the class gets the name that its new path gives. `nvs code rename --from <file>` does a list of renames in one change.
Every rename and move is checked before it changes a file. If the new code would not compile, nothing changes, and you see the error.

`nvs code unused` prints every declaration that nothing in the project uses, and `nvs code delete` deletes one. `nvs code extract`, `implement`, `inline` and `signature` do from a terminal what the editor's actions do.
The editor greys out a declaration that nothing uses, and **Delete unused** deletes it. **Inline variable**, **Inline this call** and **Inline method** replace a variable or a call with its value.

Three new editor actions ask you for text first. They change the parameters of a method, move a member to another class, and extract an interface. `nvs code signature`, `nvs code move` and `nvs code extract interface` do the same.

`Core\Mail\Message::parse` reads a raw email, such as an `.eml` file or the body of a webhook. It returns the headers, the text and HTML bodies and the attachments, and a broken message does not throw an error. Every value is tainted: it comes from outside your program, so you must check or escape it.

`Core\Mail\Message::kind` returns what kind of message it is: a bounce, a delay, a complaint, an automatic reply, a reply or other. A bounce is a message from a mail server that says your mail could not be delivered. `answers()` returns the message id of the mail it is about, so you can find the mail you sent.

`Core\Mail\Message::report` reads the delivery report in a bounce or a delay. For each recipient, it gives the address, what happened, the status code such as `5.1.1`, and whether the failure is permanent.

`Core\Imap` reads a mailbox over IMAP (the protocol a program uses to read a mailbox on a server). A program opens an `[imap.<name>]` block of `nvs.toml` by its name, and then searches, fetches, moves, flags and deletes messages. For tests, a `directory` block reads a folder of `.eml` files instead of a server.

The `[http.client.tls]` block is now `[tls.client]`. Its keys set the trusted certificates and the lowest TLS version of every outbound connection: HTTP, mail, LDAP, databases and the shared cache. When a certificate is not trusted, the error names the setting that fixes it.
entries.instead: Rename the block: write `[tls.client]` where you wrote `[http.client.tls]`. The keys `roots`, `min_version` and `keylog` are the same.

entries.text: `[debug] index_age` and `[debug] index_max` delete the records of a finished run one at a time, oldest first. Before, all the records of a finished run were deleted at the same time. The page of a run in the debug viewer says the time before which its records were deleted.

`[debug] index_max` now limits every record in the debug database, oldest first, including the records of a command that is still running. Before, the records of a running command were not deleted for size. The records of every finished request were deleted instead.
`Core\Mail::send` takes one body. A `string` is sent as plain text, and a `Core\Html\Markup` is sent as HTML with a plain text made from it. The `html` option is removed.
entries.instead: Pass the HTML as the body: write `Core\Mail::send('shop', $to, $subject, $html)` where you wrote `Core\Mail::send('shop', $to, $subject, $text, html: $html)`. Use the `text` option only to replace the plain text Novis makes.

entries.text: `Core\Mail::send` returns the `Message-ID` it wrote. New options add display names, attachments, thread headers, a one-click unsubscribe link and a bounce tag.

The CSS of an HTML mail is copied into the `style` attribute of each element it matches, because most mail programs ignore a `<style>` element. `@media` rules and rules with `:hover` stay in `<style>`. A `<link rel="stylesheet">` throws an error.
A `[mail.<name>]` block can use TLS from the first byte, a private CA, `AUTH LOGIN` and `XOAUTH2`. The `dkim_*` settings sign every message, and `capture = true` keeps each message and sends nothing.
A `[mail.<name>]` block keeps its connection open for the next message, so a second message does not need a new TLS connection or sign-in. `pool = false` opens one connection per message.
`Core\Mail::preview` builds a mail body as `send` would and sends nothing. It returns the HTML with its CSS inlined, the plain text, and the CSS rules that stayed in `<style>`.
`Core\Mail\Attachment` adds a file to a mail, from a path or from bytes. An inline image's `src()` is the `cid:` URL to write in an `` element.
`Core\Mail\Address::of` is an email address with a display name, such as `"Ada Lovelace" <ada@example.com>`. A plain string is always an address alone.
`Core\Test\SentMail` reads every part of a sent message: its `Message-ID`, the sender's name, the attachments, the thread headers, the unsubscribe link and the bounce tag.
`Core\Test\SentMail::html` returns the HTML as sent, with its CSS inlined. `text` returns the plain text as sent, which Novis makes from the HTML when the program gives none.

The debug viewer has a Mail page. It lists the messages a `capture = true` block kept. A message shows its HTML in a safe frame, its plain text, its headers, its attachments and which CSS rules stayed.

A request's page in the debug viewer shows its handler, its memory peak and limit, its response size, and the stack of an exception. Each cache, HTTP, file and process event shows its result. Sent mail and jobs pushed to a queue are events too.

The debug viewer has a Runs page. It lists scheduled jobs, queue jobs and runs of `nvs run` and `nvs test`, each with its outcome, memory, queries and dumps. A run's page has the tabs of a request's page, except Request, Response and Coverage.

`[debug] inline` adds the output of `Core\Debug::dump` to an HTML page. With `[debug] store` on, this output also shows how many queries the request ran. It has a link that opens the request in the debug viewer.

The debug viewer has a new design, with a dark and a light theme. The request list has filters, summary tiles and the time split of each request, and a request page has tabs. Two new pages show totals for each route and for each query.
`nvs debug link` prints the link to the debug viewer and starts nothing. With `--json`, it also prints the link an editor shows and whether `nvs debug` runs.

A button in VS Code opens the debug viewer in an editor tab or in your browser. The setting `nvs.debugViewer.openIn` chooses the tab or the browser. In the tab, a click on a `file:line` opens that file in the editor.

Three code lenses show what recorded requests did. Above a route handler, a lens shows the requests and their p50 duration, and above a `Core\Debug::dump` call, the newest value. Above a `throw`, it shows how often it was thrown and when it was thrown last.

`array<Status, string>` is an array whose keys are the cases of the enum `Status`. Any other key does not compile, and a `foreach` key and `Core\Arr::keys` give the keys back as cases. `$data as array<Status, string>` checks each key of an array read from JSON.

At a `match` arm, a key of an `array<Status, T>` and an argument of an enum type, completion lists the enum's cases first. At an arm and at a key, it lists only the cases you have not written yet. A quick fix adds the arms that a `match` is missing.

A `match` over an enum must handle every case. If it has no `default` arm and a case has no arm, the program does not compile (`E1016`). The error names each missing case, and the editor can add the missing arms.

A class constant and a property default can contain enum cases, `Priority::High as int`, `Foo::class` and other class constants, also inside an array. So `const array<Priority, string> LABELS = [Priority::Low => 'low']` is a table that the compiler builds once.

A method parameter of type `callable(static): bool` takes a function for the class the call names. `Order::check(fn (Order $o): bool => ...)` compiles, because the call names `Order`. Inside the method, the compiler checks `$rule($this)` and `$rule(new static())`, and any other argument to `$rule` is the error `E1015`.

`extend Core\Time\Date as BusinessDays { … }` adds methods, constants and properties to a class, an interface or an enum from `Core` or from another package. A file that writes `use` for the block can call the added methods. A call of an added method costs the same as a call of a static method.
An enum body can declare methods and constants. In a method, `$this` is the case. A static method and a constant are called on the enum, such as `Suit::count()`.

In a class, completion lists the methods of the parent classes that you can override. When you choose one, the editor writes the whole method. Its body calls `parent::name(...)` with the same parameters.

A `#[Core\Query]` parameter declared `?T $x = null` is optional, and its value is `null` when the key is missing. A `bool` query value is written `1` or `0`, and any other text gives the status `400`. A capture or a query value can be a `Core\Time\Date`, `TimeOfDay` or `Instant`, and a query value can also be a `DateTime`.

`Core\Router::url` and `Core\Uri::buildQuery` write a `Core\Time` value as its ISO text, and a `Parses` object as the text of its `format` method. `Core\Router::url` leaves out a query key whose value is `null`. A value in the `$params` array whose type the parameter cannot take, such as a `Date` for a `uint`, does not compile.
A class that implements `Parses` must now also declare `format()`. It returns the text that `parse` reads, and `Core\Router::url` uses it to write a link.
`Core\Uuid::format` and `Core\Queue\Id::format` return the text that `parse` reads. It is the same text as `toString`.
In a `final` class, `static` means that class. So a method that returns `static` may return any object of the class, such as a record that `parse` loads from a database.
A route parameter of type `Core\Queue\Id` now gets the id from the link. Before, every request to such a route gave the status `500`.
Inside `Core\Router::dispatch`, `Core\Router\Match::parameter` and `parameters` also return each converted `#[Core\Query]` value. So `Gate::allows` can check a record that a query value loaded.

A `Core\Time\Date`, `TimeOfDay`, `DateTime`, `Duration`, `Zone` or `Core\Uuid` is now a JSON string, as `Instant` already was. A time zone is written as its name, such as `"Europe/Vienna"`. A text that is not valid throws a `ParseError` that names its key.
The API document lists an optional query value as not required. A `bool` query value is the integer `0` or `1`. A `Date` has the format `date`, and an `Instant` has the format `date-time`.
A command's argument or option can be a `Core\Time\Date`, `TimeOfDay`, `Instant` or `DateTime`. The user writes it as its ISO text. A text that is not valid is a usage error.

`==` and `!=` now compare a `Date`, `TimeOfDay`, `Instant`, `Duration`, `Zone` or `DateTime` by its value, so `90m == 1h30m` is `true`. Two `DateTime` values are equal when they name the same moment, even in different time zones. Objects of every other class are still equal only when they are the same object.
`Core\Time\DateTime::compareTo` returns `-1`, `0` or `1`, by the moment of each value. So `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` now work on two `DateTime` values, also in different time zones.

`Core\ObjectMap` and `Core\ObjectSet` find a key with `==`. An equal `Core\Time` value is the same key, so `Date::at(2026, 3, 9)` finds the entry of another `Date` for that day. Objects of your own classes are still found only by identity.

`Core\Time\DateTime::fromIso` reads a text with an offset and a time zone name, such as `2026-01-05T08:30:00+01:00[Europe/Vienna]`. For such a text, the `$zone` argument is optional. An offset that the zone does not have at that time throws a `ParseError`.

`toIso()` writes a `Date`, `TimeOfDay` or `DateTime` as ISO 8601 text, such as `2026-01-05` or `08:30:00`. A `DateTime` also writes its offset and time zone: `2026-01-05T08:30:00+01:00[Europe/Vienna]`. `fromIso` reads each text back to an equal value.

`Core\Time\Date::startOf` and `endOf` return the first or last day of the date's week, month, quarter or year. `difference` counts whole days, weeks, months, quarters or years between two dates. `next` and `previous` find the nearest date on a given weekday.

A `Date` and a `DateTime` return four more calendar parts. `daysInMonth()` is the number of days in the month, and `quarter()` is `1` to `4`. `isoWeek()` and `isoWeekYear()` are the week number and its year in ISO 8601, where a week starts on Monday.

`Core\Time\Date::parse` reads a date with a pattern, such as `dd.MM.yyyy`. `Core\Time\Date::range` returns every date from one date to another, both included. Its `step` option can be a day, week, month, quarter or year.

`Core\Time\Duration::toClock` writes a duration as hours and minutes, such as `25:30` or `-1:15`. With `seconds: true` it also writes the seconds. `Core\Time\Duration::fromClock` reads such a text back to a `Duration`.
`Novis\Intl\DateFormat::Fields` selects which parts of a date are shown, such as only the month and the year. The locale decides their order, so `YearMonth` shows `Januar 2026` in `de`.

`Novis\Intl\DateFormat::dates` and `Novis\Intl\DateFormat::dateTimes` take a `fields` option, a case of `DateFormat::Fields`. On `dateTimes`, the cases without a day throw a `LogicError`. Use `dates` to show only a month or a year.

`Core\Reflect\PropertyInfo::isLateInit` returns `true` for a property declared `lateinit`. `Core\Reflect\PropertyInfo::isReadonly` returns `true` for a property declared `readonly`. Both also work for a property that the class inherits.

The server now builds the description of each class once, when it loads your program. `Core\Reflect::forClass`, `Core\Reflect::forObject` and `Core\Reflect\EnumInfo::of` return that description, so two calls for the same class return the same object. A list such as `properties()` or `methods()` is built once per request.
`nvs meta --json` writes `readonly` and `lateinit` in the signature of a property, before the type. An example is `lateinit ?Customer $buyer`.

`@see` in a doc comment can name a file in your project, and one heading of a Markdown file: `@see notes/refunds.md#who-can-get-a-refund`. The compiler checks that the file and the heading exist, and a path outside the project folder does not compile. The page that `nvs doc` writes links to the file.

In a doc comment, go to definition, hover, completion, find references and rename work on each `@see` target, `@example` path and `@throws` class. When you move a file or a folder, each `@see` and `@example` path to it changes. If a `@see` heading is not in the file, the quick fix changes it to the most similar heading.

entries.text: A `#[Core\Json\Derive]` class with a property of a `Core` class that has no JSON form, such as `Core\Uri`, stopped the program with an internal error. It is now the compile error `E0756` at that property. Declare such a property `string`, and convert the text after the decode.
`nvs agent show` prints the help of a built-in name. For an enum of `Novis\Image`, `Novis\Intl`, `Novis\Pdf` or `Novis\Spreadsheet`, it now also lists the enum's cases.

When a request calls `Core\Response::sendFile` more than once, each call replaces the earlier file. The request sends only the last file. The `max_output` limit in `nvs.toml` now counts only that file.

`Core\Str::afterPrefix` checks that a string starts with a prefix and returns the rest of the string. `Core\Str::beforeSuffix` does the same at the end. Both return `null` when the string does not match.

The warning `W1036` shows a `Core\Str::slice` that cuts off a prefix or a suffix after `Core\Str::startsWith` or `Core\Str::endsWith` tested it. It names `Core\Str::afterPrefix` or `Core\Str::beforeSuffix`, which do both in one call. When the cut is the first line inside the `if`, the editor offers a fix that writes the call for you.

`Core\Str::startsWith`, `Core\Str::endsWith` and `Core\Str::replaceAll` find a match only where it does not split a character. So `Core\Str::startsWith("e\u{301}", "e")` is `false`, because the accent belongs to the `e`. The pair `"\r\n"` is one character, so `"\r"` alone does not match inside it.
entries.instead:
To change Windows line ends with `Core\Str::replaceAll`, put the pair first: `["
" => "
", "" => ""]`. To check whether a line ends with a line break, check for `"
"` and for `"
"`.

entries.text: `Core\Str::trim`, `Core\Str::trimStart` and `Core\Str::trimEnd` remove whole characters. A character at the end is removed only when the `characters` option has every code point of it. So `Core\Str::trim("e\u{301}", { characters: "\u{301}" })` returns the text unchanged, because the accent belongs to the `e`.
entries.instead: To remove a letter with its accent, put every code point of it in `characters`, such as `"e\u{301}"`.

entries.text: You can pass `Foo::class` where a `class<T>` is expected. You do not need to write `as class<T>`. A class name in a string variable still needs `as`.

`Core\Config::set` changes only the settings on one list, and the page of `Core\Config::set` shows the list. A name you write in the call that is not on the list gives the error `E0667`. A template string that no name on the list fits gives the warning `W1037`.
entries.instead: Remove each call that sets a name not on the list. Such a call cannot change anything.

entries.text: The page of each setting says whether a request may change it with `Core\Config::set`. A page for a block lists the settings in it that a request may change.

Code in a package (a library your program installs) may change only `[limits]` settings. If code in a package writes another setting name in a call to `Core\Config::set` or `Core\Config::restore`, the call gives the error `E0667`.
entries.instead: Remove the call. In a package, it cannot change anything.

entries.text: Inside the name you pass to `Core\Config::set` or `Core\Config::restore`, the editor lists the settings a request may change. The hover on a name says how a request may change that setting.

After an edit, the editor checks fewer files. A change inside a method body or a comment checks only the file you edit. A change to a method also checks the subclasses, and for a `public` method the files that call it.

`Instant::toIso` writes a year before year 1 with four digits, such as `-9999-01-02T01:59:59Z`. `Instant::fromIso` reads this text back. JSON reads an `Instant` with the same rules as `Instant::fromIso`.
entries.instead: Read a year before year 1 as four digits after the `-`.

entries.text: In the VS Code Explorer, a file that declares one attribute shows the letter `A`. Its tooltip is "This file declares an attribute."
Inside `#[Name(`, the editor shows the fields of the attribute declaration as signature help. Each field shows its doc comment.
An attribute that nothing declares has the quick fix **Declare the attribute**. It writes an `attribute` declaration in the same file, with a field for each key you wrote.
The editor colours the words `class`, `method`, `property` and `parameter` after `on` in an attribute declaration. Each field name has the colour of a property name.
The outline lists each attribute declaration and its fields. The body of an attribute declaration folds.
The editor completes `attribute` and `repeatable` at file level and in a class or interface body. It also completes the type of each field in an attribute declaration.
Go to definition, find references, highlight and rename work on the fields of an attribute declaration. They also work on each key in a `#[Name(key: …)]` use.
`nvs code order` moves an attribute declaration in a class to the top of the class, with the `enum` and `type` declarations. **Order class members** in the editor does the same.

`Core\Csrf::token` saves no session data for a new visitor. The response still sends the session cookie, and the server accepts the token on the next request. The server saves session data only when the program writes a value with `Core\Session`.

Every use of a revoked object (an object after a call to its `revoke()` method) throws `RevokedObjectError`. This includes `.=` on a property, an `inout` property argument, a call of a method reference and `isinit`. It also includes a conversion to a string, a comparison, a `foreach`, a delegated method and a `static` call through the object.

Some decoders take a type, such as `Core\Json::decodeAs` and `Core\Request::jsonAs`. They check every class inside a shape or an array of that type, at any depth. `Core\Request::jsonAs`, `queryParametersAs` and `formFieldsAs` give the error `E0810` when such a class has a plain `string` property.
entries.instead: Write `tainted string` on each string property of a class that a request decoder reads.

entries.text: `Core\Uri::encodeComponent` throws a `LogicError` when its argument is exactly `.` or `..`. In a path, such a segment changes which resource the URI names.
entries.instead: Check the value before you encode it. For a query value, use `Core\Uri::withQueryParameter` or `Core\Uri::buildQuery`.

entries.text: The output of a child process is `tainted bytes`. The version text of a database server and the name an LDAP server returns are `tainted string`. Another program or a server writes this text, so it may contain input from outside.
entries.instead: Write `tainted` on the variable that keeps the value. Before the value goes into a path, a query or a command, convert it with a check such as `as ?int`. Or use the method that makes it safe there.

entries.text: `Throwable::$message` is `tainted string`, because some error messages contain input text. The text of a `Core\Ldap\Filter` and of a `Core\Ldap\Dn` is `tainted string` too.
entries.instead: Write `tainted string` on a variable that keeps an error message or the text of a filter or a DN.

entries.text: `Image::encode`, the pixels of `Image::raw`, each file of `Image::encodeVariants` and the result of `Pages::merge` are `tainted bytes`. An image or a PDF file may be an upload. `Font::fromBytes` takes `tainted bytes`.
entries.instead: Write `tainted bytes` on the variable that keeps the result. A response body, a file and storage all take `tainted bytes`.

entries.text: `Core\Bytes::at` takes `tainted bytes` and returns a plain `uint`. `Core\Bytes::join` takes an `array<tainted bytes>`, and the result is then `tainted bytes`.

Text from a `Core` method is `tainted` unless the method says where the text comes from. A `tainted` value passed to a parameter that does not accept `tainted` text does not compile. The error names the method that makes the value safe for that parameter.
Each task that `Core\Task::all` runs has the same capabilities and the same memory limit as the code that calls it. A task that needs more memory than the limit does not get it.
`Core\Serialize::decode` gives a revocable object that is in no collection. Encoded data cannot change which collections contain a revocable object. Data that tries throws a `ParseError`.
entries.instead: Encode the objects again with `Core\Serialize::encode`.

entries.text: When the memory limit stops a `set`, `add` or `push`, the revocable object is not added, and a later `revoke()` works as usual. `Core\Debug::dump` does not print a `#revocable` line.

A `[[restrict]]` rule covers every use of a class or method: a union type, `static::NAME`, a default value, an attribute argument and a route link. A package can restrict only its own code and the code in `Core`. A rule for any other code gives the error `E0665`.
entries.instead: Move a restriction on another package's code into that package, or into your application's `package.toml`.

entries.text: `nvs reload` exits with `1` when a server does not reply. Its line says `could not be reached` or `closed the connection without a reply`. A server that is shutting down prints a line that says it is stopping.

In development, the server checks the `Host` header of every request from a proxy on this machine. This check does not use `X-Forwarded-For`. The `421` response has a text body that names the host to add to `development_hosts` in the `[server]` block.
entries.instead: Add the host name your local proxy sends to `[server] development_hosts`.

entries.text: `Core\Test::answerHttp`, `Core\Test::answerSocket`, `Core\Test::tlsSession` and `Core\Test::scriptAnswers` throw a `LogicError` in a request, a connection, a scheduled task and a queued job. They work in a test, and in a request or a program that a test starts. They also work in a command-line program.
entries.instead: Call these methods only in a test or in a command-line program.

entries.text: A request to the test server uses the test's clock and its `env:` variables. What the request logs or sends as mail is in `Core\Test::logs` and `Core\Test::sentMail`.
A file that a response sends with `Core\Response::sendFile` counts toward the test's memory limit. A file that does not fit ends the test with a memory error.
A double can replace an interface method that has a body with a function. The double then runs that function.
`nvs test --since` also runs the tests that reach a deleted or renamed file or method. When it cannot tell which tests a change affects, it runs every test.

`toEpochSeconds`, `toEpochMillis` and `toEpochMicros` return the time since 1 January 1970, rounded down to the earlier whole unit. For example, the instant half a second before 1970 gives `-1` seconds. `Instant::fromEpoch` with the result and the remaining part gives the same instant.
entries.instead: Before 1970, add one to the result when the instant has a part of a unit left.

entries.text: `Instant::fromIso` reads an upper-case `T` and `Z`, a `.` before the fraction, and an offset with a colon, such as `+02:00`. A lower-case `t` or `z`, a comma, the second `60` or an offset like `+0100` throws a `ParseError`. So does a year that does not have four digits, such as `-009999`.
entries.instead: Write `T`, `Z`, a `.` before the fraction, and an offset with a colon, such as `+01:00`.

entries.text: `Date::fromIso('-0000-01-01')` throws a `ParseError`. Year 0 is written `0000`.
entries.instead: Write year 0 as `0000`.

entries.text: `Zone::of` gives the zone the name the time-zone database uses. `Zone::of('europe/berlin')` gives the zone `Europe/Berlin`.
The parameters of `Date::at` are named `year`, `month` and `day`.
entries.instead: Write `Date::at(year: 2024, month: 12, day: 24)`.

entries.text: `Core\Arr::append` uses the same key as `$a[] = $v`. After `unset` removes the largest number key, the next value gets the key after the removed one.
entries.instead: To number the keys again from `0`, call `Core\Arr::values` first.

entries.text: A `ParseError` from `Core\Json::decodeAs` lists at most 64 issues. When there are more, the last issue says that more follow.

A `Core\Arr` function that takes a key, such as `hasKey`, gave a compile error for a `uint` key (an unsigned whole number). It now takes a `uint` key, as `$a[$key]` already did. So `Core\Arr::fillKeys($ids, true)` works when `$ids` is a list of `uint` values.
